notes.urn:cts:latinLit:phi0474.phi050.perseus-: The sentence beginning *Cui Proserpinam* is marked corrupt (†) in the edition and lacks a main verb; '[they join]' is supplied. In 2.69 the printed *i* is taken as *ei*, 'these' [births].
The clause *quod in Libera servant, in Libero non item* ('which they keep in Libera, but not likewise in Liber') is obscure; it is translated literally.
The section breaks off mid-word (*opes mag-*); the sentence is completed in the next section ('than to have great wealth').
*rogator* is used first of the official collecting the votes, then of the presiding magistrate, Gracchus himself; each is glossed by its sense.

nodes.text: Is it not shameful, then, for a natural philosopher, that is, an observer and hunter of nature, to seek evidence of the truth from minds steeped in habit? For in that way it will be permissible to say that Jupiter is always bearded, Apollo always beardless, that Minerva's eyes are grey and Neptune's sea-blue. And indeed we admire the Vulcan at Athens made by Alcamenes, in which, as he stands clothed, a slight lameness appears that is not unsightly: so we shall regard the god as lame, since that is what we have been told about Vulcan. Come now, do we also make out that the gods have the names by which we call them?

And so, both among our people and among others, the worship of the gods and the sanctity of religious rites grow greater and better day by day; and this happens not at random or by chance, but because the gods often show their power in person, as at Regillus in the war with the Latins, when Aulus Postumius the dictator was fighting a battle against Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, Castor and Pollux were seen fighting on horseback in our battle line, and, in more recent memory, the same sons of Tyndareus announced the defeat of Perseus. For Publius Vatinius, the grandfather of this young man, when two young men with white horses had told him at night, as he was coming to Rome from the prefecture of Reate, that King Perseus had been captured that day, reported it to the senate, and at first was thrown into prison for having spoken rashly about public affairs; afterwards, when a letter had been brought from Paulus and the same day was established, he was presented by the senate with both land and exemption. And it has also been recorded that when the Locrians had defeated the people of Croton in a very great battle at the river Sagra, the news of that battle was heard at the games at Olympia on that very day. Often the voices of Fauns have been heard, often the forms of gods have been seen, and they have compelled anyone who is not dull-witted or impious to admit that the gods are present.

But among our ancestors the power of religion was so great that certain commanders even devoted themselves to the immortal gods for the commonwealth, with veiled head and in set words. I could recall many things from the Sibylline prophecies, many from the responses of the haruspices, by which those things are confirmed that ought to be doubtful to no one. And indeed the discipline both of our augurs and of the Etruscan haruspices was proved by the event itself in the consulship of Publius Scipio and Gaius Figulus. When Tiberius Gracchus, consul for the second time, was holding their election, the first *rogator* [collector of votes], just as he was reporting them [elected], suddenly died on the spot. When Gracchus had nevertheless completed the elections and perceived that the matter had become a religious scruple for the people, he referred it to the senate. The senate decided that it should be referred to those to whom [such matters] were usually referred. The haruspices were brought in and replied that the *rogator* [presiding officer] of the elections had not been lawful. Then Gracchus, as I used to hear from my father, blazing with anger:

Human life and common custom, moreover, have taken up [the practice] of raising to heaven, by fame and goodwill, men outstanding for their benefactions. Hence Hercules, hence Castor and Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence also Liber (I mean the Liber born of Semele, not the one whom our ancestors solemnly and devoutly consecrated as Liber together with Ceres and Libera, the nature of which can be understood from the mysteries; but because we call those born of us *liberi*, 'children', for that reason the offspring of Ceres were named Liber and Libera, which they keep in Libera, but not likewise in Liber)—hence also Romulus, whom some think to be the same as Quirinus. And since their souls survived and enjoyed eternity, they have rightly been held to be gods, since they were both the best and eternal.

A physical explanation, and not an inelegant one, is enclosed in these impious myths. For they meant that the heavenly, highest, ethereal, that is fiery, nature, which generates all things by itself, lacks that part of the body which needs union with another for procreation. And they meant Saturn to be the one who maintains the course and revolution of periods and seasons. This god has that very name in Greek: for he is called *Kronos*, which is the same as *chronos*, that is, a span of time. And he was called Saturn because he was sated (*saturaretur*) with years; for he is imagined to have been in the habit of devouring his own children, because age consumes the spans of time and is insatiably filled with the years that have passed. He was bound by Jupiter, so that he should not have unrestrained courses, and so that [Jupiter] might tie him with the bonds of the stars. But Jupiter himself, that is, 'helping father' (*iuvans pater*), whom in the other cases we call *Iovem*, from helping (*iuvando*), is called by the poets 'father of gods and men', and by our ancestors 'best and greatest', and indeed 'best', that is, most beneficent, before 'greatest', because it is a greater thing, and certainly more pleasing, to benefit everyone than great wealth—

The air, moreover, lying between the sea and the sky, is, as the Stoics argue, deified under the name of Juno, who is the sister and wife of Jupiter, because it has both a likeness to the aether and the closest union with it. They made it feminine and assigned it to Juno because nothing is softer than it. But I believe Juno (*Iuno*) was named from helping (*iuvando*). Water and earth remained, so that, as in the myths, there should be three kingdoms divided. So one of them, the whole realm of the sea, was given to Neptune, Jupiter's brother as we would have it, and his name was formed—as *Portunus* from *porta*, 'gate', so *Neptunus* from *nando*, 'swimming'—with the first letters slightly changed. All the power and nature of the earth, however, was dedicated to Father Dis, who is 'rich' (*dives*), as among the Greeks [he is] *Ploutōn*, because all things both fall back into the earth and arise from the earth. †To him [they join] Proserpina (which is a Greek name, for she is the one called *Persephonē* in Greek)—whom they hold to be the seed of crops, and imagine to have been hidden away and sought by her mother.

The mother, Ceres, is [named] from bearing (*gerendis*) crops, as if *Geres*, the first letter having been changed by chance, just as by the Greeks; for by them too she was named *Dēmētēr*, as if *gē mētēr*, 'earth mother'. Next, he who overturns great things (*magna verteret*) [is] *Mavors* [Mars], and Minerva she who either diminishes (*minueret*) or threatens (*minaretur*). And since in all things the first and the last have the greatest force, they wanted Janus to be foremost in sacrificing; his name was derived from going (*eundo*), from which open passageways are called *iani*, and the doors at the thresholds of secular buildings *ianuae*. For the name of Vesta [comes] from the Greeks (she is the one whom they call *Hestia*); her power extends to altars and hearths, and so with that goddess, because she is the guardian of the innermost things, every prayer and every sacrifice ends.

Not far removed from this power are the gods Penates, their name derived either from *penus* (for *penus* is everything on which people feed) or from the fact that they dwell deep within (*penitus*); hence they are also called *penetrales* by the poets. Next, the name of Apollo is Greek. They hold him to be the sun, and they think Diana is the same as the moon; the sun (*sol*) was so called either because it alone (*solus*) of all the heavenly bodies is so great, or because when it has risen all [the others] are darkened and it alone appears; the moon (*luna*) was named from shining (*lucendo*); for she is the same as Lucina, and so, as among the Greeks [they invoke] Diana, and her as Lucifera [Light-bringer], so among our people they invoke Juno Lucina in childbirth. This same Diana is called *Omnivaga*, 'all-wandering', not from hunting but because she is counted among the seven [bodies] that are, as it were, wandering;

she was called Diana because by night she made, as it were, day (*diem*). She is called upon at births, because these come to maturity in sometimes seven or, as usually, nine courses of the moon, which are called months (*menses*) because they complete measured (*mensa*) spaces; and Timaeus [put it] neatly, as [he did] many things: having said in his history that on the same night on which Alexander was born the temple of Diana of Ephesus burned down, he added that this was not at all to be wondered at, because Diana, since she had wanted to be present at the delivery of Olympias, had been away from home. The goddess, however, who came (*veniret*) to all things our people named Venus, and from her [comes] *venustas*, 'charm', rather than Venus from *venustas*.

Then Cotta said, 'Excellent. So let us proceed as the argument itself leads us. But before [I speak] about the matter, a few words about myself. For I am moved not a little by your authority, Balbus, and by that speech of yours which in its peroration urged me to remember that I am both Cotta and a pontiff; which, I believe, was meant to have me defend the beliefs about the immortal gods which we have received from our ancestors, [and] the rites, ceremonies and religious observances. I for my part will always defend them and always have defended them, and no one's speech, learned or unlearned, will ever move me from the belief about the worship of the immortal gods which I received from my ancestors. But when religion is in question, I follow Tiberius Coruncanius, Publius Scipio and Publius Scaevola, chief pontiffs, not Zeno or Cleanthes or Chrysippus; and I have Gaius Laelius, augur and also wise man, whom I would rather hear speaking about religion in that famous speech than any leader of the Stoics. And since the whole religion of the Roman people is divided into rites and auspices, with a third [element] added—whatever warnings the interpreters of the Sibyl or the haruspices have given for the purpose of prediction from portents and prodigies—I have never thought any of these observances to be despised, and I have persuaded myself that Romulus by founding the auspices and Numa by founding the rites laid the foundations of our state, which surely could never have become so great without the utmost appeasement of the immortal gods.

Nor indeed can I despise the ignorance of the common people and the unlearned when I consider the things said by the Stoics. For these are [the beliefs] of the unlearned: the Syrians worship a fish; the Egyptians have deified almost every kind of beast; in Greece, moreover, they have many gods from among human beings: Alabandus at Alabanda, Tenes on Tenedos, Leucothea, who was Ino, and her son Palaemon throughout all Greece— Hercules, Aesculapius, the sons of Tyndareus, our own Romulus, and many others, who they think were received into heaven like new and newly enrolled citizens.

One Mercury was born of Caelus [Sky] as father and Dies [Day] as mother; his member is reported to have been indecently aroused because he was excited by the sight of Proserpina; a second, the son of Valens and Phoronis, is the one who is held to be under the earth, and is the same as Trophonius; a third, born of the third Jupiter and Maia, from whom and Penelope they say Pan was born; a fourth, with the Nile as father, whom the Egyptians consider it sacrilege to name; a fifth, whom the people of Pheneus worship, who is said to have killed Argus and for that reason to have fled to Egypt and given the Egyptians laws and letters: him the Egyptians call Theyt [Thoth], and the first month of the year among them is called by the same name.

But sometimes good men do have good outcomes. Those, indeed, we seize upon and attribute without any reason to the immortal gods. But Diagoras, the one called 'the Atheist', when he had come to Samothrace and a certain friend said to him, 'You who think the gods neglect human affairs, do you not notice from so many painted tablets how many people escaped the violence of the storm by their vows and reached harbour safe?'—'That is how it is,' he said, 'for those who were shipwrecked and perished at sea are nowhere painted.' And the same man, when on a voyage the passengers, frightened and terrified by a contrary storm, told him that it was not undeservedly that this was happening to them, since they had taken him aboard the same ship, pointed out to them many other [ships] on the same course in distress, and asked whether they believed that Diagoras was being carried in those ships too. For that is how things stand: what sort of person you are, or how you have lived, makes no difference to good or bad fortune.
